Stealth addresses hide the actual destination address of blockchain transactions to enhance privacy.
DKSAP uses two pairs of keys: scan key pair (v, V) and spend key pair (s, S).
The sender generates an ephemeral key pair (r, R) for each stealth transaction in DKSAP.
DKSAP requires blockchain nodes to perform two scalar multiplications per transaction to find the destination address.
DKSAP-IoT reduces computational overhead by extending the lifetime of the shared secret for N transactions using a cryptographic hash function.
In DKSAP-IoT, only the first stealth transaction between two peers includes an ephemeral public key.
DKSAP-IoT reduces the number of random-point scalar multiplications from N to 1 on the sender side for N transactions.
DKSAP-IoT reduces the number of random-point scalar multiplications by N-1 on the receiver side compared to DKSAP.
The computational cost of hash functions is negligible compared to elliptic curve scalar multiplications.
DKSAP-IoT achieves at least 50% performance improvement over DKSAP on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B.
The elliptic curve used in implementation is sect283k1, a 283-bit binary Koblitz curve.
BLAKE-256 was chosen as the hash function for its high performance.
DKSAP-IoT provides receiver anonymity, forward privacy, and stealth transaction hiding.
Forward privacy ensures that compromising the current shared secret does not reveal previous transaction links.
Transaction size is reduced by 72 bytes per stealth transaction after the first in DKSAP-IoT.
The receiver must store private keys and transaction state encrypted to protect against device compromise.
DKSAP-IoT is motivated by TLS session resumption to improve efficiency in IoT blockchain systems.
The dual-key stealth address protocol was first implemented in 2014 for ShadowSend.
DKSAP-IoT requires both sender and receiver to maintain and update local transaction state information.
Auditors or proxy servers can scan transactions with scan private keys but cannot spend funds without ephemeral private keys.
